en: The *Ullambana Sūtra* was [expounded] when the Great Maudgalyāyana, seeking to relieve his mother, Lady Caiti, from the suffering of being suspended upside down,

established the fundamental principle of filial piety, and thus requested the Tathāgata to expound this sūtra for the benefit of all beings as a means to repay the labor and kindness of their parents.
Furthermore, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, having accumulated three great kalpas and fully cultivated filiality...
As for those who remain, they exhaust their sincerity to offer [the merit], exhorting them to resolve upon the Way;

for those who have passed away, it provides the support of sublime practice to rescue them from drowning and deliver them to the realms of humans and devas, where they may hear the Dharma and realize awakening, forever departing from the miserable destinies.

To repay this boundless debt of gratitude is not merely for the parents of this single life, but extends to the parents of immeasurable lifetimes and all six classes of relatives; thus, one repays them all. Therefore—
This refers to the Great Filial One, the Honored Śākyamuni. Those who practice worldly filial piety can only provide for their parents with warmth and coolness, sweet delicacies, and fine food;

they carefully protect their hair and skin, establish themselves in character, and bring forth a good name, ensuring their bodies are not impaired and their persons are not disgraced—this is the height of worldly filiality.
Those who practice transcendental filial piety sever their attachments and bid farewell to their kin to study the conduct of the Buddha; thus the Dharma sustains them in the present life.
I dedicate this merit to those who have passed away, so as to universally benefit all sentient beings, treating enemies and kin with equal compassion.

While the practices of Confucianism and Buddhism differ, their intent to practice filial piety is one and the same. The Chan Master Guifeng of the Tang dynasty composed one fascicle of a preface to explain the great meaning of this scripture.
To serve as a model for future generations and provide a means to repay the boundless debt of gratitude, the Great Master Yurong of Song extensively expounded upon the meaning of the commentary.

He drew extensively from the Confucian tradition, citing many instances where filial conduct was clearly manifested, thereby harmonizing the various expressions of the Way of Filial Piety into a single thread.

His work consists of two volumes titled *The Essentials of Filial Piety* (*Xiào Héng Chāo*), and he further compiled one volume of topical outlines (*kēwén*) to present its essential framework. Thus, based on the sutra...

Knowing the origins by which Maudgalyāyana initiated his teachings, he composed a *shu* (sub-commentary) to elucidate the great meaning of the sutra, and a *chao* (extract) to provide a detailed exposition of the *shu*’s text;
therein, the way of filial conduct is brilliantly and fully embodied.
At that time, in the second month of spring in the Jiyou year of the Xuande era, [he was appointed] Right Dharma Master of the Sengluosi... and so forth.
The Sub-commentary on the *Ullambana Sūtra* by the Abbot of Dàbǎo'ēn Monastery, the Śramaṇa Yīzhēn Sǒu Wéishí.
The original edition consisted of palm-leaf manuscripts (bānjiǎ):

the sūtra and its commentary together in one fascicle, the sub-commentary in two fascicles, the topical outline (*kē*) in one fascicle, and the altar ritual (*tánshì*) in one fascicle, totaling five fascicles. Now, the sub-commentary has been integrated and appended beneath the sūtra and its commentary.
It is divided into two fascicles. The structural outline (*ke-shi*) constitutes one fascicle. These are transcribed as square-format volumes and carved into printing blocks.

Generally, those with high margins are the sutras, while those with level margins are the commentaries (*shu*) and sub-commentaries (*chao*). When a title appears alone, it is a sutra; when there is a triangular mark, it is a section of the commentary.
Within these, there are circles which represent the independent interpretations of the author of the sub-commentary that do not follow the commentary. Although they are arranged...
The punctuation and collation have been completed as follows. Regarding those points where my strength was insufficient, may the gentleman who is erudite in antiquity examine them thoroughly.
